result: Old yeast cells (18-22 CBE) lose chromosomes at a frequency of 10-15%, as demonstrated by fluorescent chromosome labeling. The loss is independent of labeling method or chromosome identity, affects entire chromosomes (not just labeled regions), is fatal to cells, and occurs specifically in the last division of old mother cells.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states the findings are 'convincingly supported by carefully-designed experimental data.' Reviewer 3 describes the discovery as 'quite striking and well supported with solid experimental evidence' using 'classic microscopy-based single cell fluorescent chromosome assays that are appropriate and seem robust.' No concerns were raised about these core observations.

result: Chromosome loss in old cells occurs through asymmetric sister chromatid non-disjunction during anaphase, with 11% of anaphases showing co-segregation of sister chromatids to a single pole, and 82% of these missegregation events resulting in asymmetric partition to the bud. Non-disjoining chromatids remain attached to and co-segregate with the pre-existing (old) SPB.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this mechanistic finding. Reviewer 2 states the authors 'reveal that, in old yeast mother cells, chromosome loss occurs through asymmetric partitioning of chromosomes to daughter cells, a process coupled with the inheritance of an old Spindle Pole Body.' Reviewer 4 notes the authors 'first establish that aged mother cells exhibit aberrant error correction during mitosis.' No methodological concerns were raised about the anaphase analysis.

result: Old cells lose chromosomes due to defects in correcting syntelic chromosome attachment errors, as demonstrated by experiments with the temperature-sensitive ipl1-321 aurora B kinase mutant. The effects of age and reducing Ipl1 activity are non-additive, indicating they act through the same pathway.
evaluation: This mechanistic interpretation is accepted by reviewers. Reviewer 4 explicitly states the authors 'establish that aged mother cells exhibit aberrant error correction during mitosis' and describes the finding as 'compelling.' The ipl1-321 experiments are not questioned, and the non-additive effects support the proposed mechanism.

result: NPC remodeling and nuclear basket displacement trigger chromosome loss in aging cells. Genetic manipulations that increase ERC accumulation (sir2Δ) or destabilize the basket (mlp1Δ) promote premature chromosome loss, while interventions that prevent ERC accumulation (fob1Δ) or ERC anchorage to NPCs (sgf73Δ) suppress chromosome loss.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this causal connection. Reviewer 1 states the findings show 'aging in yeast leads to chromosome mis-segregation...driven by disruption of the nuclear pore complex.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'identify that remodeling of the nuclear pore complex (NPC), specifically the displacement of its nuclear basket, triggers these asymmetric segregation events.' Reviewer 3 states 'the correlation of this phenotype with other age-associated phenotypes - specifically extrachromosomal rDNA circles and nuclear pore dysfunction - is supported by in vivo genetic manipulations.'

result: Removing the introns from three genes involved in chromosome segregation (NBL1, MCM21, GLC7) - which are the only intron-containing genes in the chromosome segregation machinery - nearly completely suppresses chromosome loss and anaphase missegregation in old cells, extends replicative lifespan by ~20%, and has no detectable effects in young cells.
evaluation: This is described as a key finding by all reviewers. Reviewer 2 states 'Through genetic manipulation, the study demonstrates that removing introns from key chromosome segregation genes is sufficient to prevent chromosome loss in aged cells.' Reviewer 4 calls this finding 'highly compelling' and notes 'the finding that deleting the introns of 3 genes in the Aurora B pathway can suppress age-related chromosome missegregation is highly compelling.' No concerns were raised about these experiments.

result: Young mlp1Δ mutant cells (lacking the nuclear basket protein) exhibit premature chromosome missegregation with similar characteristics to old wild-type cells (fourfold increase in missegregation, 80% following old SPB), and this phenotype is suppressed by removing the three introns, demonstrating that basket defects are sufficient to cause the aging phenotype.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this as strong evidence for the causal role of basket displacement. Reviewer 4 notes 'The 3x∆i mutant also suppresses the increased chromosome loss resulting from nuclear basket destabilization in a mlp1∆ mutant.' The parallel between mlp1Δ and aging phenotypes strengthens the mechanistic model without raising reviewer concerns.

result: Old cells exhibit pre-mRNA leakage to the cytoplasm, as demonstrated by smRNA FISH showing ~70% of GLC7 intronic sequences in the cytoplasm of old cells (vs ~3% in young cells) and by a pre-mRNA translation reporter showing increased mCherry/GFP ratio in old cells. This leakage correlates with ERC accumulation (increased in sir2Δ, decreased in fob1Δ).
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 2 states 'This disruption also leads to the leakage of unspliced pre-mRNAs into the cytoplasm, highlighting a breakdown in RNA quality control.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the application of the single cell mRNA splicing defect reporter showed very convincingly that general mRNA splicing is compromised in aged cells.' Reviewer 4 states the authors 'directly test if aged cells do exhibit aberrant mRNA export, using RNA FISH to identify that old cells indeed leak intron-containing pre-mRNA into the cytoplasm.'

result: Promoting pre-mRNA leakage in young cells (hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutant) is sufficient to induce asymmetric chromosome missegregation (>10-fold increase) that is biased toward the old SPB and suppressed by removing the three introns. In contrast, spliceosome defects (snu66Δ) cause missegregation without SPB bias, indicating the phenotype is due to pre-mRNA leakage rather than splicing defects.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this as strong evidence for sufficiency. Reviewer 2 states 'Moreover, promoting pre-mRNA leakage in young cells mimics the chromosome mis-segregation observed in old cells, providing further evidence for the critical role of nuclear envelope integrity and RNA processing in aging-related genome instability.' Reviewer 4 notes 'Mutants causing increased pre-mRNA leakage are sufficient to induce chromosome missegregation, which is suppressed by the 3x∆i.' The distinction from spliceosome mutants strengthens the interpretation.

result: Introducing an artificial DNA circle (YRp17) promotes premature chromosome loss and shortens lifespan, effects that are substantially (though not completely) suppressed by the 3x∆i mutations. Similarly, the 3x∆i mutations partially suppress the premature chromosome loss and shortened lifespan of sir2Δ mutant cells.
evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about these experiments, which provide additional support for the model. The partial suppression is acknowledged in the manuscript and does not appear to concern reviewers, as it suggests both intron-dependent and intron-independent mechanisms can contribute to chromosome loss when ERC levels are very high.

result: The authors propose an integrated mechanistic model: ERC accumulation causes NPC basket displacement, leading to pre-mRNA leakage of intron-containing transcripts (NBL1, MCM21, GLC7), which impairs the aurora B error correction pathway, resulting in failed correction of syntelic attachments and asymmetric chromosome segregation. NPC remodeling is both necessary and sufficient to drive age-associated chromosome loss.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorse this integrated model. Reviewer 1 states the study 'reveals that aging in yeast leads to chromosome mis-segregation due to asymmetric partitioning of chromosomes, driven by disruption of the nuclear pore complex and pre-mRNA leakage' and that findings are 'convincingly supported.' Reviewer 2 describes the work as providing 'a compelling insight into the basis of chromosome missegregation in aged cells, tying this phenomenon to the established Nuclear Pore Complex architecture remodeling.' Reviewer 4 states the paper 'provides a compelling insight into the basis of chromosome missegregation in aged cells.'

result: Background claims about NPC remodeling in aging across species, yeast replicative aging, ERC biology, and the role of centromeres in chromosome segregation, all supported by citations to previous literature.
evaluation: These are established background facts cited from the literature. Reviewers do not question these foundational claims, which provide context for the novel findings. Reviewer 4 explicitly notes the work ties findings 'to the established Nuclear Pore Complex architecture remodeling that occurs with aging across a large span of diverse organisms.'

result: Speculative discussion about broader implications: basket displacement might affect other cellular processes beyond chromosome segregation (protein quality control, gene activation, mitochondrial function, ribosome assembly); the mechanism might be relevant to stress responses, cancer, progeria, and might represent an evolutionarily conserved response to pathogenic DNA.
evaluation: These are clearly presented as speculative implications in the Discussion section. Reviewers do not object to this speculation, which is appropriately framed as possibilities for future investigation rather than established conclusions. The speculation is grounded in the experimental findings and cited literature.
